name: Tiratricol (Triac)

lead: Tiratricol is a synthetic thyroid hormone analogue. It is approved for peripheral thyrotoxicosis in MCT8 deficiency, a rare genetic condition.
In the early 2000s it was sold in OTC fat-loss supplements. No trial has tested it for weight loss.

paras: It activates thyroid hormone receptors and can enter cells without the MCT8 transporter.
Case reports describe hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism and periodic paralysis from supplement use. The label warns against use for obesity or weight loss.

lead: Tiratricol, also called Triac or triiodothyroacetic acid, is a synthetic thyroid hormone analogue that binds thyroid hormone receptors.[1][2] It is approved in the EU and, according to a US prescribing label, in the United States as Emcitate for peripheral thyrotoxicosis in people with MCT8 deficiency (Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome).[2][3]

Outside that use, tiratricol was sold in the early 2000s in over-the-counter fat-loss supplements, and case reports describe hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism and periodic paralysis in users.[4][5][6][7] The US label carries a boxed warning that thyroid hormones should not be used for obesity or weight loss.[3]
No clinical trial has tested tiratricol as a weight-loss or appearance treatment.
infobox: Not for obesity or weight loss (US label)

paras: MCT8 deficiency is a rare genetic disorder in which thyroid hormone cannot enter the brain, producing severe neurological disability alongside high circulating T3. Tiratricol can enter cells without the MCT8 transporter.[2][3]

The label lists diarrhea, vomiting, rash and excessive sweating as the most common adverse reactions, and warns of thyrotoxicosis symptoms such as raised heart rate and insomnia, plus cross-reaction with T3 immunoassays.[3]

Case reports describe symptomatic hyperthyroidism in a person taking tiratricol as a dietary supplement,[5] hypothyroidism after use of an over-the-counter fat-loss product,[6] thyroid dysfunction from over-the-counter use in Australia,[7] and periodic paralysis.[4] Brazilian marketing authorisation was suspended in 2003, according to Wikipedia.[2] Analytical studies have also found thyroid-related compounds among adulterants in slimming products.[8]

Randomised studies in people without thyroid glands found tiratricol had stronger effects on liver and skeletal markers than on the pituitary compared with levothyroxine, suggesting tissue-selective activity.[9][10]

An international phase 2 open-label trial in children and adults with MCT8 deficiency reported that tiratricol reduced elevated T3 and addressed features of peripheral thyrotoxicosis.[1] Further registered trials include a phase 2 study in 22 patients[11] and a phase 3 withdrawal study in 20 males.[12] No studies found of tiratricol for weight loss or cosmetic purposes.

timeline.event: Randomised trial characterises organ-specific effects of tiratricol in athyreotic patients.[10]
Phase 2 trial in MCT8 deficiency published.[1]
